newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian press describes bus slaughter.
newsitem.headline: Algerian press describes bus slaughter.

text.p: Algerian newspapers on Thursday described a massacre near Algiers of at least 20 bus passengers by Moslem fundamentalists, saying they initially believed the men in uniform were security forces on a routine check.

"According to survivors, the terrorists, about a dozen, were dressed in military uniform which gave confidence to the bus driver. The group's chief, carrying a Kalashnikov rifle, entered the bus alone and asked if there were any 'colleagues' among the passengers," said Liberte newspaper.

"A young policeman presented himself. It was only when he had been seized by the pseudo-soldiers that the passengers understood. The policeman's throat was slit, then he was decapitated, then horribly mutilated."

The attack took place in Blida province, just south of the Algerian capital, in the early hours of Wednesday. Security forces earlier said 20 people were butchered and seven wounded. El Watan newspaper put the death toll at 23 and six wounded.
There has been no independent account of the attack.
The bus was stopped at a fake road block, set up between two genuine ones manned by security forces, newspapers said.
About 40 travellers were forced to get out and lie on the ground, Liberte said. The attackers then started to kill them.
"Among the victims were three women, one of them pregnant," it added. El Watan said the pregnant woman's 17-year-old daughter also had her throat slit.

It quoted a local resident as saying: "I heard a man cry with all his force 'baba' (papa), just once...then four or five gunshots...then silence. When I came out, there was the body of a man whose head had been cut off, just beside my house, and others bleeding on the other side of the road."

Rebel attacks in the first year of Algeria's conflict in 1992 focused on members of Algeria's security forces but then civilians were increasingly targeted. At first victims usually had relatives among the security forces but in what diplomats saw as an attempt to defeat harsh state censorship, leading Algerian personalities became a focus of attacks.

Their deaths were more difficult to cover up. Victims included popular singers, doctors, well-known members of political parties, and around 60 journalists or media employees whom Islamists accused of supporting the government.

Algerian officials said recent massacres aimed simply to spread fear, while diplomats suggest the killers' aims are both to defeat censorship by the horror and size of the killings which cannot be hidden, and to deny the authorities' claims that "terrorism" has been beaten.
El Watan also said five other people had been killed in Tipaza province to the west of Algiers -- two on Wednesday and three on Monday.

A resident of Algiers, speaking by telephone, also quoted witnesses as saying the body of a man, his throat cut, had been found on the pavement on Thursday near the Aurassi Hotel in central Algiers. The hotel, used for official conferences and by visiting foreigners, is opposite a Defence Ministry complex.

Security forces have been fighting Moslem rebels since the authorities in January 1992 scrapped a general election in which the Islamic Salvation Front had taken a huge lead. About 60,000 people have since been killed.
